title: Ediscovery for Social Media: The Complete Guide
summary: Top considerations and best practices for mastering data from Facebook, X (formerly known as Twitter), Youtube and other social media platforms in ediscovery.
body_markdown:
5.79 billion people participate in social media globally — and new platforms crop up every year. The scale and speed of this adoption greatly[increase the potentially relevant data](https://csdisco.com/blog/esi-collaborative-data-sources) that case teams must investigate when[conducting ediscovery](https://csdisco.com/blog/ediscovery-rules-best-practices-guide) .


However, the right skills and tech stack can help make handling social media data a breeze, speeding up your time to important information and evidence.


Keep reading for our step-by-step guide on how to do ediscovery with social media, including tips to master data collection on today’s top social platforms.


📚Unlock the[complete guide](https://csdisco.com/resource/ediscovery-expanded-ebook) of best practices for handling complex data types in ediscovery.


## **Understanding social media data**


All social media data constitutes electronically stored information (ESI) that is potentially[discoverable](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/construction_industry/publications/under_construction/2020/summer2020/sanctions-for-lost-or-destroyed-esi/) under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.


The official[Advisory Committee](https://www.gtlaw-ediscoverywatch.com/2023/03/one-district-court-observes-there-are-five-fundamental-steps-when-dealing-with-esi-discovery/) notes for the amended[37(e)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_37) in the Federal Rules even go so far as to call out this data source explicitly: *“It is important that counsel become familiar with their clients’ information systems and digital data — including social media — to address these issues.”*


**Even so, practicing attorneys still struggle with the legal scope of discoverable social media and the specific forensic methods required to preserve data from each platform.**


Below, we’ll cover the five largest platforms: Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), YouTube, TikTok, and LinkedIn.


## **Ediscovery for social media: Key challenges**


Social media ediscovery is now a routine part of modern litigation, but it brings unique challenges: Posts vanish. Formats evolve. And meaning depends heavily on context.


Unlike traditional documents, social content is dynamic, visual, and designed for mass engagement. **Here are some of the technical, legal, and procedural hurdles to be aware of when collecting and reviewing social media in ediscovery.**


### **Data collection**


Social media content moves fast, with posts disappearing, updating, or expiring automatically. That makes timely, targeted collection critical.


APIs and access policies vary by platform, and what’s public on one network might be private on another. Livestreams, stories, and comments may not be retained unless captured in real time. And while third-party tools help, they have their limitations.


Without deep platform knowledge, it’s easy to miss key content or metadata in social media ediscovery.


### **Technical preservation**


Social media content can’t simply be downloaded and stored. It has to be preserved with context, metadata, and interactive elements intact. Posts evolve‌ — ‌and across platforms like Facebook or Instagram, even small changes can complicate preservation.


To make things trickier, platform updates can break ediscovery workflows, disrupting reviewability or undermining data integrity. Smart social media ediscovery requires flexible tools that can adapt as platforms change.


### **Privacy and access**


Beyond technical challenges, accessing social media data raises legal concerns. Private messages, restricted posts, and metadata may require consent, a subpoena, or both. And global privacy laws like GDPR raise the stakes.


Parsing these issues becomes even more difficult when personal and professional accounts overlap. One account might hold work-related communications‌ — ‌but still be protected. A thoughtful approach helps you stay compliant and avoid over-collection.


### **Authentication and legal admissibility**


Courts expect evidence to be authentic, and screenshots rarely cut it. Without metadata or a clear chain of custody, even the most compelling content can be thrown out.


Proving authenticity may require more than the content itself, however. Timestamps, user details, and even forensic analysis may be needed to confirm authorship and integrity. When the source matters, so does how you collected it.


### **Review and analysis**


Reviewing social media content isn’t straightforward. Posts may include slang, emojis, or visuals that shift meaning depending on context. Threads, replies, and visual cues all matter.


You may need to reconstruct conversations, translate messages, or analyze videos while being aware that group chats can raise privilege issues. AI can help, but human review is still critical to understanding nuance and flag privilege issues.


### **Compliance and regulation**


Social media ediscovery must align with data retention laws, privacy regulations, and platform terms of service. But rules vary by jurisdiction, and improper collection can lead to sanctions or evidence exclusion.


Complicating things further, platforms may prohibit scraping or limit data access, and cross-border issues can trigger additional legal scrutiny. Defensible workflows require careful planning, legal oversight, and tools that can adapt to evolving compliance demands.


## **Social media platforms and ediscovery best practices**


Every platform comes with its own quirks. What works for Facebook ediscovery won’t work for TikTok, and what’s visible on X today might be gone tomorrow. To build a smart collection strategy, legal teams need to understand how each platform operates. To help, we’ve highlighted key considerations and practical tips for handling social media ediscovery across today’s most-used apps.


## **Facebook**


Founded in 2004, Facebook is the largest social network in the world, with[3.07 billion](https://www.statista.com/topics/751/facebook/?srsltid=AU7gw4WOvCN909hXXfch8x_9WK7Nji6XOOClE6MwX92DtbA6Fbr1ALE8#topicOverview) active users worldwide. The platform serves as a comprehensive social network that allows users to post updates, photographs, videos, classified ads, and other content, while enabling them to "follow" one another and interact through public or private comments, messages, and "likes."


Facebook also supports livestreams and permits the monetization of various content including videos, ads, and Facebook Marketplace commerce. It operates under its parent company Meta, which also owns Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp.


### **Facebook in court**


Facebook, the centerpiece of Meta Platforms, has been involved in a wide range of legal cases related to[privacy](https://www.cand.uscourts.gov/notices/facebook-privacy-settlement-information/) , antitrust,[content moderation](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/09/myanmar-facebooks-systems-promoted-violence-against-rohingya-meta-owes-reparations-new-report/#:~:text=Civil%20legal%20proceedings%20were%20filed,US'%20OECD%20National%20Contact%20Point.) ,[child endangerment](https://behindthebadge.com/social-media-platforms-sue-tech-giant-for-endangering-children/#:~:text=The%20lawsuit%20states%20that%20Meta,devices%20and%20social%20media%20platforms.) , and[use of images without permission](https://www.timescolonist.com/local-news/bc-supreme-court-approves-51m-settlement-for-facebook-users-8503032) .


Aside from Facebook’s (and Meta’s) own assorted legal embroilments, user content posted on Facebook has been used in court to show evidence of[bullying](https://www.findlaw.com/legalblogs/law-and-life/teen-sued-classmates-over-facebook-cyberbullying/) and[stalking](https://www.npr.org/2014/12/01/366534452/is-a-threat-posted-on-facebook-really-a-threat) ,[unfit parenting](https://www.carlsonattorneys.com/news-and-update/parental-fitness) , hidden income in[divorce proceedings](https://illinoislawforyou.com/blog/texts-emails-facebook-divorce-evidence/) , and[wrongful termination](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/screening-candidates-social-media-may-lead-to-tmi-discrimination-claims) , among others.


However, not all Facebook-sourced content is[admissible](https://blog.pagefreezer.com/5-times-social-media-evidence-was-denied-in-court) , and a number of challenges may have to be[cleared](https://www.findlaw.com/legalblogs/law-and-life/legal-how-to-using-facebook-as-evidence/) , such as[authentication](https://blog.page-vault.com/authenticating-social-media-evidence-federal-rules-of-evidence-901b1#:~:text=Under%20Rule%20901(b)(1)%2C%20a%20witness%20with,on%20a%20particular%20date%20and) of the content, or allegations of[hearsay](https://houstonlawreview.org/article/77679-courts-are-going-to-love-this-an-analysis-of-the-facebook-reactions-as-hearsay) .


#### **Ediscovery best practices for Facebook**


Several types of records from Facebook can be used as evidence in court, depending on the case and how the evidence is collected and presented. These may include:


- **Public posts** . Think status updates, photos, videos (including[livestreams](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/business-and-practice/court-allows-use-of-facebook-live-internet-searches-as-evidence) ), audio recordings, or comments (one’s own, or on other individuals’ content), which can be used to indicate the poster’s sentiments or intentions, actions, or even associations, such as membership in a specific club or group. If collected via[screenshot](https://blog.pagefreezer.com/collecting-online-evidence-dont-let-screenshots-sink-your-case) , such evidence would need to be authenticated.
- **Private messages** . These may be direct messages or chat logs, and generally require a subpoena or[warrant](https://www.bocalaw.com/can-text-messages-emails-or-facebook-posts-be-used-to-prove-threatening-conduct-against-me-in-court#:~:text=If%20investigators%20try%20to%20get,not%20provided%20to%20criminal%20suspects.) to be accessed – unless they’re willingly provided by a participant in the conversation.
- **Account information** . This may include friend lists (useful to establish connections between individuals of interest), Facebook group memberships, and event attendance (or intent to attend — for example, accepting an invitation).
- **Metadata** . Metadata may include time stamps on public or private posts, location data, advertising history, and even IP addresses. A[court order](https://www.facebook.com/help/494561080557017) is generally required for Facebook to disclose this information.


Privacy regulators and tech audits confirm that Facebook collects vast volumes and[types](https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/?subpage=1.subpage.1-YourActivityAndInformation) of data from its users, which it is often compelled to share with[government and law-enforcement agencies](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/14/technology/personal-data-apple-google-facebook.html) .


If you expect Facebook-generated content to become relevant to your matters, it is important to work with partners who understand the details of Facebook ediscovery, from collecting to parsing and searching such data.


#### **What about Instagram?**


Like Facebook, Instagram is part of Meta Platforms and shares similar data practices and privacy policies. While content formats differ‌ — ‌posts are more visual, stories disappear quickly, and DMs are mobile-first‌ — ‌the core ediscovery challenges remain: collecting ephemeral content, preserving metadata, and authenticating user interactions.


Instagram ediscovery often requires a different technical approach, especially when capturing stories, reels, or ad content. If Instagram activity could be relevant in your matter, work with a partner who can navigate both the platform's features and Meta’s legal response process.


### **X (formerly Twitter)**


Despite a fracturing user base, X remains a critical arena for social, political, and interpersonal discussion, operating as a social "microblogging" platform that limits messages to 280 characters. With[561 million active user](https://searchengineland.com/guide/twitter-users) s, X faces growing potential for legally actionable content, perhaps more than any other social media application.


The platform's influence has sparked the creation of competing microblogging alternatives in recent years, including Threads (an Instagram offshoot with[500 million](https://www.theverge.com/tech/950480/meta-threads-500-million-monthly-active-users-communities-your-algo) monthly active users), Bluesky, and politically influenced platforms such as Truth Social, reflecting the ongoing competition in the microblogging space.


#### **X (Twitter) in court**


X has a lengthy history in court, including[stalking cases](https://www.dallasnews.com/news/crime/2016/11/24/when-twitter-trolling-lands-you-in-jail-dallas-case-tests-limits-of-free-speech/) ,[libel and slander cases](https://globalfreedomofexpression.columbia.edu/cases/monroe-v-hopkins/) , and[inciting the London riots in 2011](https://theconversation.com/social-media-in-court-your-tweets-could-be-used-as-evidence-against-you-97739) .


In one[high-profile case](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/five-noteworthy-2020-ediscovery-cases-4486048/) related to WikiLeaks and the 2016 presidential election, X (at the time referred to as Twitter) **sought to subvert** the[Rule 45 subpoena](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_45) based upon First Amendment rights to anonymous speech. In this case, the court ruled against X because of the narrowness of the request — which excluded personal communication and demonstrated material relevance of the user’s identity — and the fact that only X itself could directly provide the information.


More recently, a federal court ruling in the trademark dispute[X Corp. v. Operation Bluebird](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/x-corp-blocks-social-media-startup-using-twitter-name-2026-09-03/) protected the "Twitter" brand name from a rival startup but simultaneously ruled that X had legally abandoned its rights to the word "Tweet" and its legacy bluebird logo.


#### **Ediscovery best practices for X (Twitter)**


Be aware of private info that requires a subpoena or court order. While some material is publicly available, accessing private data requires cooperation from the account holder or, more challengingly, X itself.


**Information not readily accessible to the public includes:**


- Password
- Email address
- Phone number or address book (which helps X suggest users you know)
- Location information (where you’re posting from)
- System log data (mobile carrier, device and application IDs, IP address, browser, the referring domain, pages visited, and[search terms](https://csdisco.com/blog/ediscovery-search) )
- Specific posts (formerly “tweets”) set as private, direct messages and deleted posts


Per X’s[FAQ on legal requests](https://help.twitter.com/en/rules-and-policies/x-legal-faqs) :


*“Obtaining non-public information, such as an email address used to sign up for an account or IP login information, requires a valid legal process like a subpoena, court order, or other local legal process, depending on the country that issues the request.*


*Requests for the contents of communications (e.g., posts, Direct Messages, media) require a valid search warrant or equivalent to be properly served on the correct X corporate entity. Law enforcement or government agents must demonstrate a higher burden of proof before a judge will authorize such a request.*


*For additional information on the types of legal process required to obtain specific types of account information, please see the “Types of Legal Process” section in our transparency report and X’s Guidelines for Law Enforcement.”*


##### **Act swiftly**


While a user's standard profile timeline only displays their **most recent 3,200 posts** , X’s Advanced Search function can bypass this limit to retrieve older public posts using specific date parameters, usernames, and keywords.


However, if a user deletes an incriminating post, it is immediately removed from public view and **cannot be recovered by the user** . X only retains deleted content on its internal server backups for a limited window of **up to 30 days** before it is permanently purged.


##### **Be specific**


Requests for data from X must be sufficiently **narrow and specific** for the social media behemoth to comply. If either of these parameters is not met, X is not afraid to fight back.


In general, the best practice with regard to X-related requests should be to ensure your request is limited to **material that is clearly relevant** to the case, **time-bound** , and **not readily accessible** from any other data source.


It is also important to include the following data points in any request:


- Username
- URL of the X profile
- Date range(s) of the requested information
- Details about the specific information being requested and its relevance to the case
- Valid email address for X to acknowledge receipt of the legal request


### **YouTube**


YouTube serves as the world's dominant video hosting platform, with over[500 hours](https://www.statista.com/statistics/259477/hours-of-video-uploaded-to-youtube-every-minute/#:~:text=Hours%20of%20video%20uploaded%20to%20YouTube%20every%20minute%202007%2D2022&text=As%20of%20June%202022%2C%20more,newly%20uploaded%20content%20per%20hour.) of user- and enterprise-generated content **uploaded every minute** and[2.7 billion](https://www.globalmediainsight.com/blog/youtube-users-statistics/#:~:text=YouTube%20has%20more%20than%202.70,world%20have%20access%20to%20YouTube.) monthly active users, making it the second-most visited website globally behind its parent company Google.


The platform generated[more than $40.4 billion](https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/youtube-generates-more-ad-revenue-than-nbcu-disney-paramount-wbd) in ad revenue in 2025, exceeding the combined total of Disney, Comcast’s NBCUniversal, Paramount Skydance, and Warner Bros. Discovery. That makes YouTube the world’s largest media company by ad revenue.


While YouTube faces competition from similar platforms such as Vimeo, Vevo, and DTube, its massive scale and integration with Google's ecosystem have solidified its position as the leading video-sharing service worldwide.


Unlike other streaming platforms, YouTube relies on users to create content and **only searches for policy violations after the fact** .


This loose approach to content regulation has exposed the organization to criticism and misuse of the platform. It has also allowed **millions** of people to **upload potentially relevant video content every day** .


Historical barriers to using video evidence — such as high costs and complex data management — have faded. Today, ediscovery platforms like DISCO provide user-friendly features such as auto-transcription and searchable time-syncing.


This wealth of potentially relevant data is increasingly prominent as a result.


#### **YouTube in court**


YouTube has faced widespread critiques ranging from[copyright infringement](https://lawstreetmedia.com/news/tech/youtube-sued-by-content-creators-for-copyright-infringement-unfair-treatment/) and[peddling conspiracy theories](https://www.theverge.com/2020/10/26/21534900/youtube-qanon-channels-conspiracy-theory-lawsuit-deplatformed) to darker things like[violence](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/09/22/former-youtube-content-moderator-describes-horrors-of-the-job-in-lawsuit.html) and sexual exploitation of[adults and minors](https://www.theverge.com/2019/2/19/18229938/youtube-child-exploitation-recommendation-algorithm-predators) .


To combat this, YouTube employs thousands of content moderators who are bombarded by questionable material every day as they strive to pull down violators. Some[former moderators have sued for emotional distress](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/09/22/former-youtube-content-moderator-describes-horrors-of-the-job-in-lawsuit.html) .


#### **Ediscovery best practices for YouTube**


In your ESI scoping, it’s important to include user-generated content on platforms like YouTube, Vimeo, and others. But as with any complex media, a solid strategy is critical.


Whether you are looking to use a video as character evidence or as direct evidence of an alleged event, the content must meet the **threshold of admissibility** for relevance and authenticity.


Even when the video has been admitted as evidence, there are some additional factors to consider in your digital evidence analysis:


##### **Take care to preserve metadata**


Even if the video is still actively being hosted on the video-sharing platform, use appropriate forensic collection technology to ensure all relevant account metadata is preserved along with the video itself.


From an authentication standpoint, information like date and time of upload, account information, and even IP address may be germane to a case.


##### **Act swiftly**


As with X, time is of the essence with YouTube requests. In the event the video in question was recently deleted, your counsel may be able to request a copy from YouTube directly, but these deleted files are unrecoverable after a period of a few weeks.


##### **Leverage AI for review**


Historically, reviewing video evidence was time- and cost-prohibitive because of the high cost of converting the media to a reviewable format and the amount of billable time it would take to review tens or thousands of hours of video.


Luckily, with today’s AI-powered tools like[DISCO](https://csdisco.com/offerings/ediscovery) , every frame of audio or video content is transcribed and converted into a format that can be searched, categorized, and analyzed for words and phrases.


AI can make connections across thousands of hours of video that would have previously been impossible.


**Note:** Transcriptions are only as good as the audio of the video. It’s still up to lawyers to validate that they’ve reviewed the relevant content.


##### **Enlist digital forensic experts to identify deepfakes**


[Deepfakes](https://security.virginia.edu/deepfakes) are AI-generated content portraying real people doing and saying things that did not actually take place. The quality of deepfakes can make it incredibly hard to distinguish them from an authentic video.


Thankfully,[digital forensic experts](https://csdisco.com/offerings/professional-services/forensic-services-collections) can identify things that are a dead giveaway that a video has been tampered with, including:


- Lens distortion
- Color filter array (CFA) artifacts
- Noise level and pattern anomalies
- Compression artifacts
- Editing artifacts


Federal statutes, state codes, and active case law are beginning to emerge in response to deep fakes.


The Take It Down Act, signed into law on May 19, 2025, represents the first major, comprehensive nationwide federal deepfake legislation. It explicitly criminalizes the nonconsensual publication of intimate images and digital forgeries. Its strict “notice-and-removal” mandate took effect May 19, 2026, forcing websites and apps to establish a formal system to purge reported deepfakes within a strict window.


The No Fakes Act is federal legislation that specifically targets the unauthorized commercial monetization of AI-generated copies of a person's voice or physical likeness.


As of late 2026, 47 U.S. states have passed at least one statutory law targeting deepfakes in three statutory buckets:


- Intellectual property and music (the Elvis Act)
- Elections and political ads
- First amendment blowback


In addition, civil courts are aggressively applying traditional common-law doctrines to synthetic media, including defamation, right of publicity, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.


### **TikTok**


TikTok arrived in the U.S. in 2017 and has gained immense popularity as a social media platform that allows users to create, edit, share, and discover short videos ranging from[dance challenge](https://www.tiktok.com/@bdash_2/video/6716540825989287173?refer=embed) s to insider tips on[home inspections](https://www.businessinsider.com/tiktok-home-inspector-flipped-home-renovation-red-flags-2021-1) .


With over[136 million](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/tiktok-stats/) unique users monthly[users](https://www.linearity.io/blog/tiktok-statistics/#:~:text=TikTok%20generated%20an%20estimated%20$9.4,revenue%20contributing%20$11.65%20billion%E2%80%8B.&text=As%20of%202023%2C%20TikTok%20had,end%20of%202024%E2%80%8B%E2%80%8B.) in the U.S. and a user base largely[under 35](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/01/31/americans-social-media-use/) , TikTok has become so influential that it has prompted competing platforms‌ — ‌including those that pre-date it‌ — ‌to adopt similar short-form video functionality, such as Instagram Reels (which has[500 million daily active users](https://www.demandsage.com/instagram-statistics/) ) and YouTube Shorts. Like Instagram and Facebook, TikTok also offers "live" feeds, further expanding its multimedia capabilities and cementing its position as a major force in the social media landscape.


#### **TikTok in court**


TikTok’s availability in the United States was challenged in 2025 by the threat of a U.S. ban unless ByteDance divested its U.S. operations.


It wasn’t until January 22, 2026, that ByteDance spun off its American operations into a new majority American-owned joint venture, with a coalition of U.S. investors assuming a combined 80% majority ownership stake. Oracle manages the app’s source code, algorithm, and American user data to satisfy federal security requirements.


TikTok is increasingly used to **share and spread information** from all around the globe. It has a popular TikTok “Live” function, wherein creators can live-stream a video feed and receive virtual “[gifts](https://www.zdnet.com/article/how-to-go-live-on-tiktok/) ” that can be converted to real-world currency. And the economic complications don’t stop there. TikTok generates[$28.4 to $34.8 billion](https://www.shopify.com/blog/tiktok-ad-spending) in advertising[revenue](https://www.yaguara.co/tiktok-ad-revenue/#:~:text=The%20TikTok%20ad%20revenue%20is,reach%20%2411.01%20billion%20in%202024.) . Popular users frequently post[sponsored content](https://www.vox.com/recode/23197348/tiktok-ad-sponcon-influencers) . And nearly 7.5 million U.S. businesses have a presence on the app, including some that use the[TikTok Shop](https://www.npr.org/2024/02/08/1228226459/tiktok-shop-amazon-social-media-business-ecommerce) feature.


Much like YouTube, TikTok videos may be used as[evidence](https://www.kenneylegaldefense.us/2023/02/20/tiktok-crimes-activity-challenge/#:~:text=Recording%20criminal%20activity%20on%20TikTok,of%20the%20act%20in%20question.) of individuals’ actions and whereabouts. But beyond basic evidence, the app's copycat nature has turned into a massive legal minefield for corporate entities.


Because TikTok structurally rewards users for remixing the exact same trends, filters, and sounds, lines are constantly blurred around copyright, likeness rights, and unauthorized reuse.


What started as a harmless dance challenge has now evolved into real-world litigation. For example, music labels like[Universal Music Group](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/anajuneja_lawyer-tip-if-your-brand-uses-trending-share-7455269288367788032-Nqtk/) have launched multi-million dollar lawsuits against major retail brands for using trending user audio in commercial ads without a proper license. State regulators are also stepping in, aggressively[suing the platform](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/international/us/daily-time-limits-filter-controls-and-account-privacy-tiktok-agrees-to-platform-level-changes-for-teens-settles-lawsuit-with-alabama-for-100-million-days-before-trial/articleshow/134497508.cms?from=mdr) for designing these copycat loops to be intentionally addictive to minors. For legal practitioners, navigating TikTok means recognizing that when a brand participates in a viral trend for commercial gain, it could easily trigger a costly copyright or advertising claim.


#### **Ediscovery best practices for TikTok**


TikTok, like many next-gen social media platforms and communication applications, is nothing like a traditional “document.”


The **public data** collected from TikTok posts may include:


- The video or photograph(s) posted
- Description text
- Closed caption text (whether auto-generated or manually created)
- Dynamic user interaction data, such as likes and comments
- Filters and sounds used to create the post
- Metadata about the user and the posting


In addition, TikTok stores numerous data points that are **not publicly visible** . These can include:


- Profile and post views
- Account and viewer activity analytics
- Direct messages (DMs)
- Saved live-streams (with accompanying data, such as chat logs and recorded “gifts” sent to the broadcaster)
- Creator’s revenue from TikTok


Collecting from a platform like TikTok can involve a number of legal considerations, such as the location of any implicated users, appropriate retrieval of the post data, and establishment of chain of custody.


If you expect a matter to involve the collection and review of TikTok data, it is crucial to engage a partner with deep experience in ediscovery for social media, who can provide a platform that facilitates intelligible review of the relevant content.


### **LinkedIn**


Launched in 2003, LinkedIn emerged as a platform for professional networking, allowing users to build online resumes and connect with potential employers and colleagues.


LinkedIn was designed to function as a digital resume, allowing users to showcase their work experience, skills, and accomplishments. But it soon transcended its original purpose, serving as a space for industry news, thought leadership, and even virtual socializing. Many describe it as the “[Facebook of business](https://www.quora.com/Is-LinkedIn-the-Facebook-of-business) ,” signifying its wide global reach and cultural significance.


LinkedIn currently has over[1.3 billion members](https://news.linkedin.com/2026/linkedin-reaches-the-milestone-of-100-million-users-in-brazil) in more than 200 countries and territories worldwide. The United States has the most members, with over[261 million](https://www.google.com/search?q=how+many+people+participate+in+social+media+globally+2026&sca_esv=4c5de4241442eb86&biw=1115&bih=831&sxsrf=APpeQnt8Oe8UmXI8n9zKsrLQ9zikVEUcLg%3A1790345373554&ei=LXq2ap-bLNKgqtsPxorFuAw&uact=5&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&fbs=ABfTbFVyMZGZf1hfvX9uKjN_-G8cY2oODYyTyZk24Xz37_7FQzcgMAXI6mDl4aLs1WJDXE-FPuVUjVB9_WO7OnpH1X7GhGoNVLROZYTxoyoqEaYuHoimt3pWXb53g23_AG9i1E3-FqvwcOEhEsN7FK5D_TL-ALc6u0EHzr2A8DQywTWiDtiNpbCzh-gpEsfSeAE1Jhk89paPewcMKf3xe6ky6HKoknlVYA&aep=10&ntc=1&mstk=AUtExfDTsE1uIPrS5pRHosVT_vjkZFyd7Pgh-VREWzZGj0avdfXE3DdJrp_RP4-e2TPca7K7RB32ZYCRfMwoULgFG0l7fjrIbQ-Vjj5vkJ-T1_wzSU2Q6qw7xiCYx1RCj0w1XX9v3K-2xhUj0yPCCM6C_CR2Y0EaILGBZIith0COdvIO1fZtCXLb6dzYbIeRtERf4iXvKPb_9lK5Tp14JAofKoM-e4OfT0J1EI6XESB-7eNrOXPzLmdtSYg89w&aioh=3&csuir=1&cs=0&mtid=3IK2aoLjK_zdwN4P7POP8Qc&udm=50) , followed by India with[186 million](https://espirian.co.uk/linkedin-membership-numbers/) .


### **LinkedIn in court**


Although LinkedIn has not faced as many legal actions as Facebook or other social media entities, it has been involved in court cases regarding[data scraping](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/LinkedIn-Wins-Latest-Court-Battle-Against-Data-Scraping/635938/) , where the legal boundaries of accessing public profile information are debated.


Content posted on LinkedIn‌ — ‌publicly, privately, or anywhere in between‌ — ‌can potentially be used as[evidence in court](https://www.wnj.com/updates/using-linkedin-evidence-in-court/) , just like any other social media content. For instance, LinkedIn posts have been used to establish witness credibility (or lack thereof) and in[employment disputes](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/case-law-alert-use-employer-employees-linkedin-profile-d%C3%A9borah-attali/) .


### **Ediscovery best practices for LinkedIn**


Much like other social networking platforms, LinkedIn hosts a number of data categories, including public content (posts, articles, comments, reactions), private content (chats, messages), account information, and metadata pertaining to all other types of content.


While LinkedIn activity is more likely to fall on the professional, public-facing side, the business-related nature of the platform means that LinkedIn content could easily prove to be valuable, or even dispositive, in a legal action.


LinkedIn presents itself as a tool to grow one’s business. It was rated the #1 platform for B2B lead generation, and more than[67.1 million](https://business.linkedin.com/advertise/ads/audience) companies and organizations have a page on the platform. It is certainly feasible that, in the event any of these companies were accused of malfeasance, LinkedIn content could be brought in as evidence.


So far, **LinkedIn content has been used in court cases far less than evidence collected from other platforms** , but it is always worth considering this possibility and working with a partner who has experience with LinkedIn ediscovery.


## **Overview: A strategic approach to social media ediscovery**


When conducting social media ediscovery, understanding how your clients use these various platforms will enable you to construct a plan to manage the growing data volumes.


### **Where do you look for social media data?**


The key to determining which technology to investigate is to **understand how relevant custodians are communicating, and on which platforms** .


Understanding the nature of a case, and if and how custodians are leveraging social media, helps determine the priority of discovery. Plus, many businesses use these platforms for their communications, so this applies to businesses as well as individual employees.


### **What do you look for?**


Every social media account holds a massive mix of data going all the way back to day one. Because of that, you need to know exactly what your tech partner is pulling during a capture — and what metadata they are leaving behind.


**User-generated social media ESI may include:**


- Engagement data (for example, a user’s posts, likes, and comments)
- Direct messages
- Chat logs
- Friends or connections
- Profile
- Log-on and posting times
- Location data from photographs
- Some deleted materials


**System-generated social media ESI may include:**


- Proprietary unique identifier
- Item type
- Parent item/thread
- Recipients
- Author/poster
- Linked media
- IP addresses
- Location data from IoB and IoT devices


### **How do you collect social media ESI?**


While it may be enticing to print out a screen capture of a public social media site, or even have the account owner press the “download your data” button offered by several platforms, **the output is unlikely to include all the useful or relevant data** , and it may be limited to only public posts.


Additionally, some social platforms limit what you are able to export based on the type of account a user maintains. Working with a[forensic collection technology](https://csdisco.com/offerings/professional-services) that specializes in social media collection will ensure you are able to gain access to the full scope of potentially relevant information. It is also important to work with a technology that can render ‌social media data into an easily reviewable format.


When collecting social media data, keep in mind that the format of the collection is paramount to ease of review, and not all collections are created equally. Some third-party collections may not do a good job of presenting the information in an easily digestible and easily producible matter.


Good and consistent collection of data = easy review and production


### **When can you use social media ESI?**


While there is ample precedent and case law to support the inclusion of social media ESI (even data that is private) in a discovery request, the requesting party still has an obligation to meet the requirements of[FRCP 26(b)](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/external/document/XFGQEGQO000000/litigation-overview-rule-26-b-and-discovery-scope-discovery) and demonstrate relevance to the case.


And the bar for relevance,[Federal Rule of Evidence 401](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre/rule_401) , is far from high. Evidence is relevant if “it has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence” and “the fact is of consequence in determining the action.” To ensure that this does not become a fishing expedition, the court will often limit subject matter and duration of admissible ESI.


An additional area of concern with social ESI in particular is authentication — meaning, the account and material posted to it were actually generated by the custodian or named account owner. As with relevance, the bar is not terribly high.


[Federal Rule of Evidence 901](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre/rule_901) states that to establish authenticity, “the proponent must produce evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims it” and this is done via presenting the “distinctive characteristics” of an account according to 901(b)(4). These characteristics may include account name, photos of the account owner, nicknames, IP address, specific topics, or slang. Keep in mind: this type of information is only available if the data was properly collected.
